new_statements.quote: Stress is not predictable in the case of words of more than two syllables. [...] Words of two syllables are invariably stressed on the final syllable. [p.29] Words of three syllables may be stressed on either the ultimate or penultimate syllable. [...] Stress may occur on any of the last three syllables of the word, but uninflected forms are frequently stressed on the final syllable. [p.30] 2.2. OLGOL, OKUNJAN, KAWARRANGG. The remarks already made on the structure and stress pattern of Oykangand words also apply in general to the other dialects. [...] OLGOL. [...] Monosyllabic words [...] become di-syllables in final position. The stress in this case falls on an additional final vowel [p.31]

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: ANU/Pacific Linguistics B-11 scan with text layer) plus its. Checked both the text layer and rendered page images (page render, printed pp. 29-32 = PDF pp. 33-36). Every quoted sentence is on the page verbatim: p. 29 under the sub-heading 'Stress Pattern' (section 2.1 OYKANGAND): 'For most Australian languages, stress occurs regularly according to a predictable pattern.. usually on the initial syllable of the word. By contrast, there is evidence in Kunjen for a strong phonological pressure against this stress pattern. Stress is not predictable in the case of words of more than two syllables.' and 'Words of two syllables are invariably stressed on the final syllable' (intYim 'house', amay 'b…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress (perceived as intensity) falls on one nuclear syllable per phonological word and, in Sommer's Kunjen data, is not predictable in words of more than two syllables: disyllables are always stressed on the final syllable; trisyllables on the final or the penult with no preferred pattern (sub-minimal pairs such as iɲáŋar 'aunt' vs. anaŋár 'pushed apart'); four- and five-syllable words on any of the last three syllables, uninflected forms most often final. Sommer states explicitly that this description, made on Oykangand, applies in general to Olgol; the Olgol-specific exception is that phrase-final monosyllables acquire an extra final vowel that carries the stress, while some Olgol speakers keep the stress on the initial syllable in that case. Blevins 2001:485 reports second-hand that the Olgol recorded by Rigsby 'shows consistent stress on V2' (second syllable).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed as such; reduplicated grammatical compounds 'retain stress on both elements' and are treated as two phonological words (p. 30).
new_statements.exceptions: Monosyllables show stress only inside multi-word phrases; Olgol phrase-final monosyllables become disyllables with stress on the added final vowel (partially devoiced), but some Olgol and a few Oykangand speakers keep initial stress in such forms (pp. 31-32); high-frequency phrase-initial modifiers lose their initial vowel (p. 29). Conflicting second-hand report: Rigsby's Olgol has consistent second-syllable stress (Blevins 2001:485); Alpher 1976 (per Blevins) argues against a V2-stress analysis for Oykangand-Olgol.
new_statements.domain_note: Phonological word (one to five syllables, coinciding closely with the grammatical word); the description is based on Oykangand tape corpora with Olgol, Okunjan and Kawarrangg corpora checked against it; isolation forms (responses to lexical cues) and phrase-final position behave differently in Olgol.
new_statements.identity_note: Olkol [olk] (olko1234, Glottolog Bookkeeping) = Sommer's 'Olgol', the Alice River people's lect, one of the Kunjen dialects (Glottolog language kunj1245 Kunjen [kjn], whose listed dialects are Oykangand oyka1239, Ogh Awarrangg ogha1238, Ulkulu ulku1238 -- Sommer 2006:7 says Olgol is NOT the Ulkulu of Ebagoola); Hamilton 1997 calls it Uw Olkola, a sister dialect of Uw Oykangand with 97% core cognacy. The quoted stress description in Sommer 1969 is written for Oykangand (oyka1239) and is extended to Olgol by the author's explicit statement in section 2.2 (p. 31), with Olgol-specific exceptions given there; the ISO code [olk] was created in 2013 (CR 2012-062) on AUSTLANG/Bowern grounds, and Glottolog considers it the same language as Kunjen (Dixon 1970).

sources.note: p. 485: Alpher (1976:86-7) argues a stress-shift (V2) analysis is impossible for Ogunyjan and Oykangand-Olgol because V2 has been reduced/deleted; Sommer's Uw-El sister dialects have initial (V1) stress on all roots; 'The Olgol recorded by Rigsby, on the other hand, shows consistent stress on V2' (second-hand from Rigsby's data; Blevins reads Rigsby's Olgol as a conservative dialect). p. 488 table: Olgol initial-dropping 'invariable', sources Sommer 1969 and Alpher pers. comm.
